newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland peace process in doubt after arms vote.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland peace process in doubt after arms vote.

text.p: Britain and Ireland were struggling to keep their 14-month-old Northern Ireland peace process on track after the the province's Protestant politicians embarrassingly rejected key proposals on the surrender of guerrilla arms.

"It's clearly a setback, but I don't think it's a long-lasting setback," former U.S. senator George Mitchell, the chairman of the peace talks, told reporters after Protestant unionists voted the plan down.
The vote dashed hopes that a compromise was imminent on the surrender of guerrilla weapons after 14 months of deadlock and painstaking Anglo-Irish diplomacy.

The unionists, guardians of continued British rule of the province, rejected the plan because it would have allowed the Irish Republican Army's political wing, Sinn Fein, to take part in talks on a political settlement without surrendering any of its guns and bombs.

The IRA ordered a truce at the weekend in its 28-year war against British rule, but unionists tended to dismiss the ceaesfire as a mere ploy to enable Sinn Fein to attend peace negotiations due to start on September 15.
Two small unionists parties walked out of the talks after the vote and the mainstream Ulster Unionist Party insisted that it would not negotiate with Sinn Fein while its IRA allies remain armed.

The unionists fear the IRA, one of the world's most experienced guerrilla organisations, will return to violence unless the talks lead to the united Ireland, a prosepct which Northern Ireland's Protestants staunchly reject.

Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam and Irish Foreign Minister Ray Burke said they would press ahead with plans for political negotiations on September 15 and would work behind the scenes for a compromise on surrendering guerrilla arms.

"The talks process goes on. Both governments are firmly committed to substantive political negotiations on 15 September. We will hold to that and will take all necessary steps to ensure that that happens," Mowlam said.
The two governments were backed by U.S. President Bill Clinton's administration which has solidly supported Anglo-Irish attempt to reconcile pro-British loyalists and Irish Catholic nationalists.
"We regret that vote," State Deparment spokesman James Foley told reporters. "I think the important point, though, is that the process will continue. We don't see this vote as an end of the process."

Mitchell said the talks would be formally adjourned until September after a session on Monday and hoped that a plan on surrendering weapons could be reached to allow negotiations to start in September.

"I believe if we can get to the point where there is genuine substantive discussion and the establishment of even the minimum level of trust necessary for reasoned argument to be made and listened too, then a settlement could be reached," he said.

But the talks lost their first participants when the Democratic Unionist Party of Ian Paisley and Robert McCartney's UK Unionist Party walked out in protest at what they said were plans to appease the IRA and Sinn Fein.
"We have now left this particular process because there is nothing in it for unionists...and those who believe in law and order. The gunmen have taken over the process," Paisley told reporters.
